entries.topicDescription: Type-safe abstractions and reified type parameters in inline functions.

tips.title: Declaration-site variance vs use-site variance solve the same problem differently
tips.content:
Declaration-site variance (`class Producer<out T>`) marks a type as
covariant everywhere it's used, once, at the class definition — every
consumer of Producer<T> automatically benefits from the covariance.

Use-site variance (`fun copy(from: Array<out T>, to: Array<T>)`) applies
the variance annotation only at a specific usage site, for a type that
wasn't declared variant at all — necessary for types like Array, which
can't safely be declared covariant in general but can be treated as such
for a specific read-only parameter.
tips.codeSnippet:
class Producer<out T>(private val item: T) { fun get(): T = item } // declaration-site

fun <T> copyArray(from: Array<out T>, to: Array<T>) { // use-site — Array itself is invariant
    for (i in from.indices) to[i] = from[i]
}

tips.title: @UnsafeVariance overrides variance checking for provably safe cases
tips.content:
A covariant type parameter (`out T`) normally can't appear in an `in`
position (as a function parameter) anywhere in the class, since that
would break variance safety in the general case — but sometimes a
specific method is provably safe despite the position, such as
List<T>.contains(element: T) checking equality rather than actually
storing the value.

@UnsafeVariance suppresses that compiler check for a specific parameter,
which is how the standard library itself defines methods like
contains() on the covariant List<out T> interface — use it only when
you've manually verified the usage can't actually violate variance
safety.

tips.title: F-bounded polymorphism lets a generic bound reference the type parameter itself
tips.content:
A recursive bound like `<T : Comparable<T>>` is called F-bounded
polymorphism — the bound constrains T to types that are comparable
specifically to themselves, not to some other unrelated type, which is
exactly the guarantee needed for a generic sort or max function to be type-
safe.

This pattern also shows up for fluent, self-referential builder APIs
where each builder step must return the same concrete subtype it started
with, not just the base builder type.

tips.title: Combine multiple unrelated bounds on the same type parameter with where
tips.content:
A single `<T : Bound>` only expresses one constraint directly after the
colon — when a generic function genuinely needs a type argument to
satisfy two or more unrelated interfaces simultaneously (both Comparable
and a custom Auditable interface, say), a single bound syntax can't
express that.

The `where` clause lists every required bound for the same type
parameter, all of which the compiler enforces must be satisfied
together by any type argument at the call site — distinct from listing
multiple type parameters, which would constrain unrelated types instead
of the same one.

tips.title: Model existential-style 'some type, but I don't care which' with a sealed wrapper
tips.content:
Kotlin doesn't have Java's wildcard-heavy existential type syntax
directly, but the same need — holding a value of some unknown but
consistent type, without exposing that type to callers — can be modeled
with a sealed wrapper class hiding the type parameter behind a non-
generic interface.

This is useful for heterogeneous collections where each entry has its own
internal type, but the container itself only exposes type-erased
operations to the outside.

tips.title: Self-referential generics enable type-safe fluent builder chains
tips.content:
A fluent builder base class whose methods return the base type loses type
information as soon as a subclass-specific method is called — the
returned base type doesn't expose the subclass's own methods, breaking
the chain.

Combining F-bounded generics with an abstract self() function preserves
the concrete subclass type through every chained call, so
`CarBuilder().configure().withColor("red")` type-checks correctly instead
of needing an explicit downcast partway through the chain.

tips.title: Variance annotations constrain the public API, not internal implementation
tips.content:
Declaring a class covariant (`out T`) only restricts how T can appear in
the class's public member signatures — it says nothing about how T is
used in private implementation details, where the compiler doesn't
enforce variance rules at all.

This means a covariant class can freely store T in a private mutable
field internally (an 'in' position), as long as no public method exposes
T in an unsafe 'in' position — the variance contract is about the API
surface callers see, not the private mechanics behind it.

tips.title: Use-site type projections (List<out T>) restrict a call site, not the whole type
tips.content:
MutableList<T> is invariant by declaration, so a function parameter typed
MutableList<Animal> can't accept a MutableList<Dog> even though Dog is an
Animal — but a specific function might only ever read from that
parameter, never write to it, making the invariance unnecessarily
restrictive for that one use.

A use-site projection (`list: MutableList<out Animal>`) tells the
compiler 'treat this parameter as covariant just for this function,' by
restricting the parameter to only read (out) operations within that
function body, without needing to change the class's own declaration.

tips.title: Nothing is the bottom type — a subtype of every generic instantiation
tips.content:
Nothing has no instances and represents 'this code path never completes
normally' — but as a type, it sits at the bottom of Kotlin's entire type
hierarchy, meaning List<Nothing> is a subtype of List<out T> for every
possible T, which is exactly why emptyList() can be assigned to a
List<String>, List<Int>, or any other list type without casting.

Understanding Nothing as the bottom type (rather than as 'no type')
explains why functions that always throw can be used anywhere a value of
any type is expected — the compiler treats 'never returns' as compatible
with every possible return type.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun emptyList(): List<Nothing> = ArrayList() // List<Nothing> is a subtype of every List<T>

val strings: List<String> = emptyList() // compiles — List<Nothing> fits List<String>
val ints: List<Int> = emptyList()       // also compiles, same reasoning

tips.title: Generic constructors can introduce type parameters independent of the class
tips.content:
It's easy to assume all of a class's generic behavior comes from its
class-level type parameters — but a specific constructor (or a secondary
constructor) can declare its own type parameters, scoped only to that
constructor's own parameter types, separate from the class's own generic
parameters.

This is a narrow, advanced feature mostly relevant to library-style
factory constructors that need to accept a differently-typed argument
than the class itself is parameterized over, without exposing that
second type parameter on the class as a whole.

tips.title: Generic classes let one implementation work across many types
tips.content:
Without generics, you'd need a separate class for IntBox, StringBox,
UserBox, and so on, duplicating identical logic for each type just to get
type safety.

A generic class parameterized with <T> writes the logic once, and the
compiler substitutes the concrete type at each usage site — giving you
both code reuse and compile-time type checking, instead of choosing
between the two.

tips.title: Type inference usually removes the need to write generic type arguments
tips.content:
Explicitly writing `listOf<String>("a", "b")` or
`val box: Box<Int> = Box<Int>(5)` is redundant when the compiler can
already determine the type parameter from the arguments or the assignment
target.

Let the compiler infer the type argument from context whenever possible;
only write it explicitly when there's genuine ambiguity, such as calling a
generic function with no arguments to infer from (`emptyList<String>()`).
tips.codeSnippet:
val names = listOf("Ahmed", "Ali") // inferred as List<String>, no <String> needed

val empty = emptyList<String>() // explicit needed — nothing to infer from

tips.title: out and in mirror producer/consumer roles, not just direction
tips.content:
`out T` means the type is only ever produced (returned) by the generic
type, never consumed (taken as a parameter) — this makes List<out T>
covariant, so List<Dog> can be used where List<Animal> is expected.

`in T` is the opposite: the type is only ever consumed, making the generic
type contravariant. Comparator<in T> is contravariant because a
Comparator<Animal> can safely compare Dogs — remembering 'producer =
out, consumer = in' (PECS) makes variance rules predictable instead of
memorized.

tips.title: Star projections when you don't care about the exact type argument
tips.content:
Sometimes you need to accept a generic type but genuinely don't use its
type parameter — like a function that just checks a List's size regardless
of what it holds. Writing List<Any> is wrong because List<String> isn't a
List<Any> without covariance rules kicking in awkwardly at call sites.

List<*> (star projection) says 'a List of some unknown type,' letting you
call methods that don't depend on T (like size) while the compiler still
prevents you from unsafely calling methods that would require knowing T.

tips.title: Upper bounds restrict a type parameter to a known hierarchy
tips.content:
An unbounded type parameter <T> only lets you call Any's methods on T
inside the function body. An upper bound (<T : Comparable<T>>) tells the
compiler T is guaranteed to have specific members, unlocking type-safe use
of those members without casting.

This is how generic utility functions like max/min-of-comparable work —
the bound guarantees compareTo exists without needing a runtime check.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b

maxOf(3, 7)          // works — Int is Comparable<Int>
maxOf("a", "b")       // works — String is Comparable<String>
// maxOf(SomeClass(), SomeClass()) // compile error unless SomeClass implements Comparable

tips.title: Generic type erasure blocks reified-free runtime type checks
tips.content:
Without reified (which only works on inline functions), a generic function
can't check `if (value is T)` or instantiate T directly, because the JVM
erases T to its upper bound (usually Any?) at runtime.

When you need runtime type info in a non-inline context (e.g. a class
method, not a top-level inline function), pass a KClass<T> explicitly as a
parameter instead of relying on the erased type parameter.

tips.title: Multiple bounds via a where clause combine several constraints
tips.content:
A type parameter sometimes needs to satisfy more than one interface — for
example, being both Comparable and Serializable. A single `<T : Bound>`
syntax only allows one bound directly after the colon.

The `where` clause lets you list multiple upper bounds for the same type
parameter, all of which must be satisfied by any type argument used at the
call site.

tips.title: Prefer generic functions over Any parameters for compile-time safety
tips.content:
Accepting Any and casting internally (as? T) defers type errors to runtime
and loses IDE autocomplete/refactoring support at call sites, even though
it looks flexible.

A generic function signature keeps the compiler checking types at every
call site — reserve Any (and unchecked casts) for genuine
type-erasure-driven interop code, like a generic event bus that must accept
heterogeneous payload types.

tips.title: Generic functions and classes
tips.content:
Generics let you write code that works with any type while keeping type safety.
Use angle brackets <T> to declare type parameters.

The compiler ensures you only use operations valid for that type.
Without generics, you'd need to cast from Any — losing safety.

Common conventions: T for type, E for element, K/V for key/value,
R for return type.

tips.title: reified type parameters
tips.content:
On JVM, generic types are erased at runtime — you can't check
'is T' or get T::class inside a generic function.

Kotlin's 'reified' keyword fixes this for inline functions.
The compiler inlines the actual type at each call site,
so the type information is preserved at runtime.

This enables type-safe APIs that would be impossible in Java.

tips.title: Variance — in, out, and star projection
tips.content:
Variance defines subtyping relationships for generic types.
'out' (covariant): Producer<out T> — can only produce T, not consume.
'in' (contravariant): Consumer<in T> — can only consume T, not produce.

'out' means: if Dog extends Animal, then List<Dog> is a subtype of List<Animal>.
'in' means: if Dog extends Animal, then Comparator<Animal> is a subtype of Comparator<Dog>.

Star projection (*) means "I don't know or care about the type parameter."
